common_name: Summer Wave Large Amethyst Torenia (Trailing Large-Flowered Shade Wishbone Flower)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed into moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; this Suntory-bred trailing selection carries noticeably larger flowers than the original Summer Wave line.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, well-drained, fertile soil in shade to partial shade, where the trailing stems cascade attractively from baskets, window boxes, and raised bed edges. Summer Wave Large Amethyst was bred to carry markedly larger, richer-purple tubular flowers than the standard Summer Wave series while keeping the same self-cleaning, heat-tolerant trailing habit, so no deadheading is needed to keep it blooming from spring into fall. It handles heat and humidity better than most shade-flowering annuals, though soil kept too wet can invite root rot, so ensure containers and beds drain freely between waterings. Give plants a light monthly feeding to sustain the long, continuous bloom period.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Summer Wave Torenia series notes
University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions — Torenia

common_name: Summer Wave Large Blue Torenia (Trailing Large-Flowered Shade Wishbone Flower)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in filtered light to shade; this vigorous trailing selection can spread up to 3 feet, so give baskets and beds ample room.

directions: Site in filtered sun to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, and expect a vigorous trailing habit that can spread up to three feet from a compact 8-10 inch tall crown. Summer Wave Large Blue produces true deep blue-purple, four-petaled tubular flowers with an orange-blushed throat in far greater profusion than seed-grown torenia, blooming from spring to frost without any deadheading required. It thrives in the high humidity and heat of southern summers, making it one of the more dependable shade trailers for hanging baskets and window boxes where hummingbirds are frequent visitors. Keep the root zone evenly moist but not waterlogged, since torenia is prone to root rot in soggy soil.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Summer Wave Torenia series notes

common_name: Catalina Gilded Grape Torenia (Yellow Bicolor Wishbone Flower)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost in bright shade to partial sun; the unusual yellow-and-purple flower color pairs well with blue- and violet-flowered torenia companions.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright, filtered sun, where it forms a mounded, trailing plant well suited to combination containers and hanging baskets. Catalina Gilded Grape is prized for its unusual golden-yellow flowers marked with a deep purple throat and wishbone-shaped stamens, a striking departure from the blues and violets typical of the genus. It flowers continuously from planting until frost without deadheading, tolerates summer heat and humidity well, and resists deer browsing, though consistent moisture prevents the leaf scorch that can occur if plants dry out in full sun. Light monthly feeding keeps the display full through the season.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Annuals for Shade

common_name: Kauai Deep Blue Torenia (Compact Shade Wishbone Flower)

planting.note: Transplant after frost danger passes into moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Kauai series stays compact and mounded rather than trailing, making it ideal for shaded bed edging.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the compact mounded habit fills in bed edges and container fronts without sprawling. Kauai Deep Blue bears royal blue tubular flowers with sky-blue overtones, a white throat, and a small yellow flare, blooming from late spring into early fall on a plant that stays notably tidier than trailing torenia types. It was selected as a Louisiana Super Plant for its reliable performance through Gulf South heat and humidity, requiring no deadheading to keep flowering steadily. Avoid letting the soil dry out, since torenia foliage and flowering both decline quickly under drought stress.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Louisiana Super Plants program

common_name: Endless Illumination Browallia (Reblooming Blue-Purple Bush Violet)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this vegetatively propagated series reblooms without deadheading through the hottest part of summer.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part to full shade, where the mounded habit fills containers, hanging baskets, and shaded borders. Endless Illumination bears lavender-blue, star-shaped flowers in continuous flushes all season on a heat-tolerant plant that needs no deadheading to keep reblooming. Unlike many flowering annuals it performs best with restrained feeding, roughly once a month, since heavy fertilization can push foliage at the expense of flowers. If the leaves show signs of sun scorch, move containers to a shadier spot, since this cultivar prefers the low, filtered light typical of shade gardens.
sources: Proven Winners — Endless Illumination bush violet

common_name: Endless Flirtation Browallia (White-Flowered Reblooming Bush Violet)

planting.note: Plant after the last frost in part to full shade (4 hours of direct sun or less) in evenly moist, well-drained soil; the pure white flowers brighten deeply shaded beds and containers.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade, since this cultivar tolerates as little as four hours of direct sun and prefers dappled or filtered light. Endless Flirtation produces abundant pure white, star-shaped flowers with a small buttery-yellow eye in a dense, mounded form, blooming continuously all season without any deadheading needed. It shows notably strong heat tolerance for such a shade-loving plant, making it a dependable choice for hanging baskets, window boxes, and shaded flower beds through the peak of summer. Water regularly to prevent the soil from drying out, which can cause flowering to stall.
sources: Proven Winners — Endless Flirtation bush violet

common_name: Angelface Wedgwood Blue Angelonia (Bicolor Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil; the bicolor dark-purple-and-white blooms add contrast among solid-colored angelonia plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, where the upright spikes add structural height to beds, borders, and large containers. Angelface Wedgwood Blue produces bicolored blossoms of deep purple and white on extra-large snapdragon-like spikes carried on a semi-upright, well-branched plant, with a faint grape-soda fragrance noticeable up close. It shares the Angelface series' outstanding heat, humidity, and drought tolerance, blooming from spring through frost with minimal disease pressure and without any deadheading required. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching, and feed on a regular schedule to sustain the heavy, continuous bloom through the hottest months.
sources: Proven Winners — Angelface Wedgwood Blue angelonia
